batchName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE) - Medium Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE)

questions.question: Why does the modern challenger distrust the ancient claim that the allies fought for citizenship?
options: The only sources were Sulla's self-serving memoirs
Writers under the emperors projected their own high value of citizenship onto the past
The surviving coins openly reject Roman citizenship
The ancient writers were all Samnites hostile to Rome
Ancient writers had no access to Roman records
questions.explanation: Under the emperors, citizenship was a prized privilege, so later writers assumed the allies craved it. Yet his view has not won everyone over.
questions.sourceQuote: He argues that writers living under the emperors, when citizenship was a prized privilege, projected their own values onto the past.

questions.question: How did Sulla's reforms weaken the tribunes of the plebs?
options: Their number was cut to just two
Their term was halved to six months
They lost the power to propose laws
They were appointed by the Senate
The office was abolished entirely
questions.explanation: Tribunes could no longer propose laws, and former tribunes could hold no further office. Sulla's aim was to rebuild the state in the Senate's favour.
questions.sourceQuote: Tribunes lost the power to propose laws, and former tribunes could hold no further office.

questions.question: According to ancient writers, how did Sulla die in 78 BC?
options: He was thrown from his horse near Puteoli
He burst a blood vessel shouting for an official to be strangled
He was poisoned by surviving supporters of Marius
He was stabbed by a proscribed man's son
He was killed by his own mutinous troops
questions.explanation: Ancient writers say Sulla burst a blood vessel in a rage at a corrupt local official. It was Cinna, not Sulla, who was killed by mutinous troops.
questions.sourceQuote: According to ancient writers, he burst a blood vessel while shouting for a corrupt local official to be strangled.

questions.question: What fuelled allied anger after 133 BC?
options: New Roman taxes imposed on allied harvests and livestock
Roman support for popular uprisings against local elites
A ban on allied soldiers sharing in the plunder of war
Roman officials seizing land guaranteed by treaty to give to poor citizens
Roman demands that the allies build and crew war fleets
questions.explanation: Roman reformers began handing out public land to poor citizens, much of it long left in allied hands. Italian communities complained their treaty rights were being violated.
questions.sourceQuote: Italian communities now complained that Roman officials were seizing property their treaties guaranteed.

questions.question: Why was an offer of Roman citizenship less simple for the allies than it might sound?
options: Citizenship required moving permanently to the city of Rome
New citizens had to pay a heavy entry tax to the Roman treasury
A person could hold only one citizenship, so becoming Roman meant giving up one's own community
Only speakers of Latin were allowed to be enrolled as citizens
New citizens lost the right to own land in their home towns
questions.explanation: Because citizenship was exclusive, becoming Roman meant abandoning one's own community. Several proposals to offer the allies citizenship failed before the war.
questions.sourceQuote: Even that offer was complicated, because a person could hold only one citizenship.

questions.question: Which groups were excluded from the 89 BC law extending Roman citizenship to almost all Italians?
options: Marsi and Picentes of the Apennines
Latins and Etruscans of central Italy
The townspeople of Asculum and Nola
The Greek cities of southern Italy
Samnites and Lucanians still in the field
questions.explanation: Only the Samnites and Lucanians still fighting were left out. A stubborn band of them fought on until 87 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Only the Samnites and Lucanians, a people of the far south, still in the field were excluded.

questions.question: What happened to Drusus, the reforming tribune whose laws at some point included citizenship for the allies?
options: He was exiled to Africa by the Senate
He became the first consul of Italia
He was murdered by an unknown assassin
He was executed after a treason trial
He was killed by the rebels at Asculum
questions.explanation: Drusus's complicated package of laws collapsed, and he was murdered by an unknown hand in 91 BC. The allies had already been preparing in secret, exchanging hostages.
questions.sourceQuote: His measures collapsed, and Drusus was murdered by an unknown assassin.

questions.question: What did Marius gain from his secret deal with the tribune in 88 BC?
options: The command against Mithridates
Command of the siege of Asculum
The office of dictator
The governorship of Africa
A consulship for the following year
questions.explanation: Marius backed the voting law in exchange for Sulla's eastern command. Armed gangs filled the streets, and Sulla even had to shelter in Marius's house.
questions.sourceQuote: Marius would back the voting law, and in return the tribune would transfer the war against Mithridates to Marius.

questions.question: While governing a province in Asia Minor, Sulla became the first Roman official to meet an envoy of which power?
options: Armenia
Numidia
Pontus
Parthia
Ptolemaic Egypt
questions.explanation: Parthia was the great power beyond the Euphrates. Sulla met its envoy while governing in Asia Minor, modern Turkey.
questions.sourceQuote: There he became the first Roman official to meet an envoy of Parthia, the great power beyond the Euphrates.

questions.question: Why did the Romans call the Social War the "Marsic War"?
options: After the Marsic Way, the road the rebels held
After Mars, the war god the rebels swore by
After the Samnite word for an allied soldier
After Marius, the general who led Rome's defence
After the Marsi, a mountain people east of Rome
questions.explanation: The Romans named the war after the Marsi. The modern name comes from the later Latin bellum sociale, "war of the allies."
questions.sourceQuote: Romans called the conflict the Marsic War, after the Marsi, a mountain people east of Rome.
